name: Wyoming

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt from state and local sales taxes, candy and soft drinks included, since July 1, 2006.

Alcohol is taxed at the general rate, state and local, in stores and served; Wyoming has no separate alcohol or local meals tax. The Liquor Division's wholesale markup (up to 17.6%) and the excise taxes by volume are left out here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the general rate, state and local (no exemption in W.S. 39-15-105; the Department of Revenue's Nicotine Products bulletin says they are "also subject to sales tax when sold at retail"), on top of excise taxes (60 cents a pack of cigarettes, 20% of the wholesale price of other tobacco, 60 cents an ounce of moist snuff, 15% of the wholesale price of vapor products), which are left out here. State law bars cities, towns and counties from imposing their own taxes "upon the sale" of nicotine products (W.S. 39-18-103(b)). County sales taxes are counted all the same: counties levy them under the state's sales tax law, which gives them exactly the state tax's exemptions (W.S. 39-15-202 and 39-15-205), the Department of Revenue's rate charts give one rate for all taxable sales, and its sales tax rules say "retail sales of all nicotine products shall be subject to the sales tax in addition to the tax imposed by W.S. 39-18-103" (Department of Revenue Rules, chapter 2, section 12(s), effective May 20, 2026). No published ruling, Department notice or court case takes up the two laws together.
Barber and beauty services: not taxed, since Wyoming's sales tax reaches only the services the law lists (W.S. 39-15-103(a)(i)), and these are not among them.
Laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: taxed (W.S. 39-15-103(a)(i)(J), repair labor; Department of Revenue Rules, chapter 2, section 12(o), laundry and dry cleaning).

Gasoline and diesel are exempt from the sales tax and pay 24 cents a gallon instead, left out here. From July 1, 2026, electricity sold at DC fast charging stations also pays a license tax of 3.5 cents a kilowatt-hour instead of sales tax (2026 HB 145; W.S. 39-17-301(a)(iii), 39-17-304(a)(iv), 39-15-105(a)(v)(E)); home and other charging isn't covered.
Clothing is taxed, with no sales tax holiday; diapers and menstrual products are taxed.
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus a 5% state lodging assessment and up to 2% in local lodging taxes, which are not counted here.
gaps: The Teton Village and Grand Targhee resort districts levy 2% (Grand Targhee 3% from January 1, 2027) on all taxable sales and services in their small districts (Department of Revenue map); each is far less than half of census tract 56039967602, which keeps Teton County's 3%.

Changes from January 1, 2027 (Department of Revenue, January 2027 rate chart): Crook County 1% to 2%, Fremont County 1% to 1.75%, Laramie County 1% to 2% and the Grand Targhee Resort District 2% to 3%. The rates here are current through December 2026; each county's page says so.

County sales tax questions on the November 3, 2026 ballot, by the county clerks' unofficial counts (canvasses pending). Approved: new 1% specific purpose taxes in Park, Johnson (two of three projects) and Uinta counties and an added 0.5% general tax in Washakie County from July 1, 2027; continuations of the 1% general tax in Albany, Campbell, Carbon, Laramie, Natrona, Sheridan and Washakie counties. Rejected: Converse County's 1% general tax and Goshen County's 0.25% economic development tax, which state law ends after June 30, 2027. A new tax can begin April 1, 2027 at the earliest and none is yet on a Department of Revenue chart; current rates are used here, and each county's page gives its counts. Sweetwater County's specific purpose tax is reported to end after December 2027 (news report).

Wyoming cities levy no sales tax of their own today; Casper's 1% (April 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026) has ended. There are no local meals or alcohol taxes, and lodging taxes (a 5% state assessment and up to 2% local) are outside these categories.

56001: Albany County's local sales tax was 2% through June 30, 2026, 1% from July 1 to September 30, 2026, and is 2% again from October 1, 2026, with the specific purpose tax voters approved on May 5, 2026 (Department of Revenue rate charts). Voters continued its 1% general tax, 9,148 to 3,824, and its 2% lodging tax, 10,325 to 2,580, for January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2030, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (county notice; County Clerk's unofficial count). The current 2% is used here.
56005: Voters continued Campbell County's 1% local sales tax on the November 3, 2026 ballot, 7,608 to 3,593 (county notice; County Clerk's unofficial count). The current 1% is used here.
56007: Voters continued Carbon County's 1% general tax, 2,841 to 1,374, and its 2% lodging tax, 3,457 to 761, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (the County Clerk's sample ballot and County Clerk's unofficial count); with its 1% specific purpose tax the county's local rate stays 2%, which is used here.
56009: Voters rejected the continuation of Converse County's 1% general tax (the 5th Penny) on the November 3, 2026 ballot, 1,948 to 2,415, and renewed its 2% lodging tax, 3,189 to 1,162 (election proclamation of August 19, 2026; County Clerk's unofficial count). State law ends a county tax voters reject after June 30 of the next year, here June 30, 2027 (W.S. 39-15-203(a)(i)(D)), when the county's local sales tax would fall from 1% to none; neither the county nor the Department of Revenue has yet posted an end date. The current 1% is used here.
56011: Crook County's local sales tax fell from 2% to 1% on April 1, 2025, and rises to 2% on January 1, 2027 with a new specific purpose tax (Department of Revenue rate charts, January 2027 chart); the rates here are current through December 2026.
56013: Fremont County's local sales tax fell from 1.5% to 1% on April 1, 2025, and rises to 1.75% on January 1, 2027 with a 0.75% economic development tax, which was on the August 18, 2026 primary ballot (Department of Revenue rate charts, January 2027 chart; County Clerk's election proclamation); the rates here are current through December 2026.
56015: Goshen County's local sales tax is 1.25%: a 1% general tax and a 0.25% economic development tax (Department of Revenue rate charts). Voters rejected continuing the economic development tax for four years on the November 3, 2026 ballot, 2,203 to 2,299 (corrected election proclamation of September 16, 2026; County Clerk's unofficial count). State law ends an economic development tax voters reject after June 30 of the next year, here June 30, 2027 (W.S. 39-15-203(a)(v)(D)), when the county rate would fall to 1%; neither the county nor the Department of Revenue has yet posted an end date. The current 1.25% is used here.
56019: Johnson County's local sales tax is 1%. A new 1% specific purpose tax was on the November 3, 2026 ballot as three propositions, each standing alone (the County Clerk's sample ballot). By the County Clerk's unofficial count, voters approved $280,000 for streets in Kaycee (1,902 for, 1,611 against) and $5,748,696.71 for North Burritt in Buffalo (1,826 for, 1,648 against) and rejected $5,000,000 for Rock Creek and Johnson Creek roads (1,691 for, 1,770 against), so the tax is to raise $6,028,696.71; it can begin April 1, 2027 at the earliest (W.S. 39-15-207(c): the first day of a quarter after 60 days' notice to sellers); the Department of Revenue has not yet posted it. The current 1% is used here.
56021: Laramie County's local sales tax fell from 2% to 1% on April 1, 2026, and rises to 2% on January 1, 2027 with a new specific purpose tax, 6% in all across the county (Department of Revenue rate charts, January 2027 chart); the rates here are current through December 2026. Voters renewed its 1% general tax (the 5th Penny), 19,212 to 11,109, and its 2% lodging tax, 22,232 to 7,985, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (County Clerk's notice of election, August 6, 2026; County Clerk's unofficial count).
56025: Voters continued Natrona County's 1% general tax (the 5th Penny), 14,997 to 7,049, and its 2% lodging tax, 17,719 to 4,213, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (county election proclamation; County Clerk's unofficial count). The current 1% is used here.
56029: Park County levies no local sales tax. Voters approved a new 1% specific purpose tax on the November 3, 2026 ballot, 6,596 to 5,138 (County Clerk's unofficial count), to raise $19,278,000 for projects in Cody ($9,800,000, the auditorium), Powell ($7,900,000, a senior center) and Meeteetse ($1,578,000), ending once that sum is collected (county sample ballot); it can begin April 1, 2027 at the earliest (W.S. 39-15-207(c): the first day of a quarter after 60 days' notice to sellers); the Department of Revenue has not yet posted it. The current 0% is used here.
56033: Voters continued Sheridan County's 1% general tax, 7,485 to 4,507, and its 2% lodging tax, 8,782 to 3,040, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (the County Clerk's general election proclamation and County Clerk's unofficial count); with its 1% specific purpose tax the county's local rate stays 2%, which is used here.
56037: Sweetwater County's 1% specific purpose tax is reported to reach its collection target in December 2027, after which it ends (Sweetwater Now, December 2, 2025, a news report); the county's November 3, 2026 ballot carried no sales tax question, only its 2% lodging tax, which voters renewed, 9,162 to 1,737 (the County Clerk's proclamation and County Clerk's unofficial count). Neither the county nor the Department of Revenue has posted an end date for the specific purpose tax, so the current 2% is used here.
56039: Teton County's local sales tax rose from 2% to 3% on April 1, 2025 (Department of Revenue rate charts); the current rate is used here, though the spending figures are for 2024.
56041: Uinta County's local sales tax is its 1% general tax. Voters approved Proposition 2 on the November 3, 2026 ballot, 3,419 to 2,672 (County Clerk's unofficial count), a 1% specific purpose tax for $13,000,000 of emergency equipment (communications, fire trucks, water tankers, ambulances and protective gear) that the ballot called a continuation; the Department of Revenue's charts from April 2023 to January 2027 list no specific purpose tax in Uinta County, so it adds 1% once it starts, and it can begin April 1, 2027 at the earliest (W.S. 39-15-207(c): the first day of a quarter after 60 days' notice to sellers); the Department of Revenue has not yet posted it. The current 1% is used here.
56043: Washakie County's local sales tax is its 1% general tax. Voters continued it from July 1, 2027, 1,951 to 805, approved an added 0.5% general tax from July 1, 2027 for ambulance and emergency medical services, 1,880 to 884, and renewed the 2% lodging tax, 2,149 to 562, on the November 3, 2026 ballot (the County Clerk's sample ballot and election proclamation of August 13, 2026; County Clerk's unofficial count). The county rate would be 1.5% from July 1, 2027, the date on the ballot (the Department of Revenue has not yet posted it); the current 1% is used here.
5613150: Casper levied its own 1% city sales tax (W.S. 39-15-204(a)(vii)), 6% in all, from April 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 (Department of Revenue rate charts; voters approved it in November 2024). It has ended, and the current 5% is used here; the spending figures are for 2024, before it began.
5675935: Two resort districts levy a tax of their own on all taxable sales and services in them (Department of Revenue rate chart): the Teton Village Resort District 2% (9% in all) and the Grand Targhee Resort District, at the ski resort near Alta, 2% (3% from January 1, 2027). Each is a small area on the Department of Revenue's 2026 Miscellaneous Districts map, far less than half of census tract 56039967602, which holds the Teton Village and Alta CDPs and takes Teton County's 3%, so the districts' rates are not in these figures.

programs: Downtown development authorities are mapped for Casper, Laramie and Rawlins from the Department of Revenue's 2026 Miscellaneous Districts layer, and for Cheyenne from the Cheyenne and Laramie County GIS Cooperative's layer; Cheyenne's four urban renewal plan areas (Hitching Post, 15th Street, Hynds and The Hole, and West Downtown, adopted 2021 to 2023 and running to 2046 to 2048) from the same cooperative. Wyoming Main Street names nine programs (accredited: Gillette, Laramie, Rock Springs and Sheridan; affiliates: Douglas, Evanston, Glenrock and Torrington; candidate: Afton) but publishes no district boundaries, so none are mapped.

warn.text: Laramie draws many visitors (the University of Wyoming and travelers on Interstate 80), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Gillette draws visitors (travelers on Interstate 90 and energy-industry workers who stay in its hotels), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}; the lodging in those tracts likely serves coal and oil workers more than tourists. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Cheyenne draws many visitors (Cheyenne Frontier Days each July, the state capitol and Interstates 25 and 80), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Casper draws visitors (the National Historic Trails Interpretive Center, Casper Mountain and Interstate 25), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

programs: Casper's Old Yellowstone District urban renewal area (the Casper Urban Renewal Agency's plans of 2002 and 2016) isn't mapped: the city publishes no boundary layer for it.

Rawlins' visitor caution draws on 25 lodging places (3.2 per 1,000 residents) along Interstate 80, which likely serve travelers passing through and workers more than visitors who stay, so read that caution with care.

Little America's page is built from a census tract it shares with Granger and James Town; the tract's visitor caution draws on its 11 lodging places (3.7 per 1,000 residents) along Interstate 80, which likely serve travelers passing through more than visitors who stay, so read that caution with care.

Buffalo's visitor caution draws on its 21 lodging places (3.2 per 1,000 residents) where Interstates 25 and 90 meet, which serve travelers passing through as well as visitors to the Bighorn Mountains, so read that caution with care.

Wright's page is built from a census tract whose visitor caution draws on its seasonal homes (211 of 1,088, 19.4%), unusual for a coal-mining town; the Census counts homes kept for occasional use as seasonal, which here may be housing for mine workers more than vacation homes, so read that caution with care.

warn: Converse County's store sales on this site (the model's estimates for 2024) come to about 26% of the taxable sales the state reports for the same kinds of stores there (the mean of fiscal 2024 and 2025), against a median of about 71% for Wyoming's counties; Wyoming counties under half that median carry this note. 74% of the state's figure there is Miscellaneous Retail (about 43% statewide), a group whose sellers the state's report doesn't name. The cause wasn't confirmed (the state's figure may include sales to businesses), so read the county's store figures with care: they may understate how much shopping happens in the county.

Goshen County's store sales on this site (the model's estimates for 2024) come to about 22% of the taxable sales the state reports for the same kinds of stores there (the mean of fiscal 2024 and 2025), against a median of about 71% for Wyoming's counties; Wyoming counties under half that median carry this note. 63% of the state's figure there is Miscellaneous Retail (about 43% statewide), a group whose sellers the state's report doesn't name. The cause wasn't confirmed (the state's figure may include sales to businesses), so read the county's store figures with care: they may understate how much shopping happens in the county.
